name: Old and Middle Welsh
confidence_why: Willis 2009, Morris-Jones 1913, Evans 1964 and Watkins 1972 all put Old and Middle Welsh word stress on the penult; they differ only on when the earlier final-syllable prominence gave way to it (Morris-Jones 1913 dates the shift to early Middle Welsh, Watkins 1972 much earlier) and on whether that earlier stage was final stress or only final high pitch.

catalog_quote: [Willis 2009 sec. 2.1.6] Late Brythonic had penultimate stress, which became word-final stress as the result of the loss of word-final syllables. In Old Welsh, the stress accent shifted back to the penultimate syllable, although the pitch accent remained word-final, resulting in the dissociation of stress and pitch accent characteristic of Welsh today. ... The date of the accent shift has been the subject of dispute. Morris-Jones (1913: 48) thought it occurred in early Middle Welsh (twelfth to early thirteenth century). Conversely, Watkins (1972, 1976) considers it to have occurred much earlier than this, perhaps in the ninth century ... This supports an Old Welsh (ninth-century) date for the accent shift. new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's penult rule for the period in which Welsh has word stress, and adds (a) a claimed earlier Primitive Welsh stage with no contrastive stress and a final-syllable high pitch, (b) the persistence of final high pitch alongside penultimate stress. It implicitly rejects the older account (Jackson 1953) of a final STRESS accent in Old Welsh that shifted to the penult c. 11th century: for Watkins the finality was pitch, not stress. Note the open copy is the Études celtiques congress summary, not the BBCS 25 article; the date he assigns to the rise of penultimate stress is not visible.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Watkins argues that Primitive Welsh had no contrastive stress at all (stress evenly spread over all syllables) but a pitch contrast with higher pitch on the final syllable; at a later date (which the paper's second part tries to fix, on the unreadable p. 429) stronger stress developed on the penult, while the high pitch stayed on the final syllable, as in Modern Welsh. So the stage with word stress is penultimate; the earlier stage is 'no contrastive stress + final high pitch'.
new_statements.exceptions: none in the visible page; the date at which penultimate stress appeared (the paper's second part) is on p. 429, which could not be read
new_statements.identity_note: Watkins' summary speaks of 'Primitive Welsh' (the pre-Old Welsh stage) and of the later development of the penultimate accent that survives in Modern Welsh; it does not name a dialect. The Persée item is a two-page congress summary (Actes du quatrième congrès international d'études celtiques, Rennes 1971) of the BBCS 25 article, not the article itself, and it also mentions a companion piece, 'The accent-shift in Old Welsh', in the Sommerfelt memorial volume ed. H. Pilch.

readall_conflicts: Watkins 1972 (as summarised on p. 428 of the Études celtiques abstract) disagrees with the standard Jackson 1953 account that the catalog's Willis-based record implicitly rests on: Jackson has a final stress accent in early Old Welsh (after apocope) shifting to the penult around the 11th century, whereas Watkins holds that Primitive Welsh had no contrastive stress at all, only a higher pitch on the final syllable, and that penultimate stress arose later while final high pitch persisted; the date he gives is on the unread p. 429. Both agree that the language with word stress has it on the penult, which is what the catalog rule (penultimate stress) encodes; the disagreement is about the earliest stage (final stress vs. no stress + final pitch) and about the date of the penultimate accent. Jackson could not be opened, so its side is not quoted here. No disagreement on placement: everything opened or held by the project gives regular penultimate word stress for Old and Middle Welsh once a stress accent exists, matching the catalog rule (penultimate stress). The one difference is about the PRE-shift stage and is between sources, not with the classification: Willis 2009 (following Jackson 1953) describes late Brythonic penultimate stress becoming word-FINAL stress after the loss of final syllables and then retracting to the penult in Old Welsh, whereas Watkins 1972 (congress summary p. 428) argues Primitive Welsh had no contrastive stress at all, only word-final high pitch, with p…

audit.reasoning: Both deciding quotations were re-opened in the copies we hold and match verbatim at the stated sections/pages (one silently dropped sentence in the Willis excerpt, no change of sense). The classification (MW penultimate stress, right edge, weight-blind; earlier OW final stress noted in the secondary-stress rule; listed exceptions from Morris-Jones sec. 41) rests on a 2009 specialist chapter with a dedicated stress section plus the standard 1913 historical grammar, and is uncontroversial in the field. Two Glottolog-listed grammars downloaded now (Evans 1964 GMW, Falileyev 2008) either presuppose penult accent or defer the topic; neither contradicts. Remaining unheld works (Jackson 1953, Watkins 1972, Schrijver 1995) bear only on the dating of the OW accent shift, already represented in the secondary-stress rule, so no reclassification or re-read is needed.
